Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.

   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate — Because the study uses repeated cross-sectional household surveys rather than a longitudinal panel, individual panel attrition does not apply, and item-level missingness in the 1996/2001 and 1996/2005 probit regressions is low (<3%; Table 2 vs. Table 12). However, 1996 water expenditure data were completely unavailable, preventing any pre- vs. post-privatization affordability comparison (Section 3(c), p. 5), and survey sample sizes shrank markedly across waves (especially El Alto n = 56 in 2001; Table 2, p. 3).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious — Privatization was non-randomly adopted across only four cities (two treated: La Paz and El Alto; two comparators: Santa Cruz and Cochabamba). Pre-reform coverage trends (1992-1996) differed substantially across cities (Table 7, p. 7; Figure 4, p. 8) and were not controlled in the DiD regressions; household covariates were restricted to log per-capita income (potentially endogenous; Note 17, p. 13) or only three basic dwelling variables due to cross-survey incompatibility (Note 18, p. 13); time-varying city-level economic/demographic shocks and differential population growth were unadjusted; and standard errors were not clustered at the city level (only 4 clusters).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate — The legal, contractual, and regulatory architecture of Bolivia's water concessions (1906 Ley de Aguas, 1994 Ley 1600, 1997 Regulation of Concessions, Laws 2029/2066 creating SISAB, contractual expansion targets, tariff dollarization, elimination of communal standpipes, and the 2005 SISAB independent audit) is well documented in Section 2 (pp. 2-3) and Notes 3-9 (pp. 12-13). However, the quantitative DiD analysis operationalizes exposure as a coarse time-invariant city binary ('privatized' vs. 'non-privatized') that codes Cochabamba as non-privatized despite its 1999-2000 Aguas del Tunari privatization, 35% tariff hike, and 'water war' cancellation.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Serious — Survey definitions of 'piped water' changed between the pre-privatization surveys (1992 and 1996, which specified piped water from the utility network inside the dwelling or yard) and the post-privatization surveys (2001 and 2005, which recorded generic 'piped water' without specifying inside dwelling/yard or utility vs. private network; Table 4, p. 4). Surveys also could not separate protected from unprotected wells/boreholes, and affordability relied on self-reported prior-month expenditure without water quantity consumed, confounding price changes with consumption adjustments and post-privatization metering/billing of previously free connections (pp. 5, 10; Note 21, p. 13).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak to Moderate — Household water access and monthly water expenditure are drawn from official national household surveys (INE), avoiding investigator-induced recall bias, but cross-wave questionnaire non-equivalence in water-source categories (Table 4, p. 4), lack of data on water quality, pressure, or continuity, absence of 1996 baseline expenditure data, and lack of volumetric water consumption substantially limit outcome measurement validity.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: No information — No pre-analysis plan or pre-registered protocol is mentioned. Although the authors report both short-run (1996-2001) and longer-run (1996-2005) DiD estimates, two covariate specifications (Table 12, p. 11), and sensitivity across Kakwani effort-appreciation parameters (e = 0.1, 0.5, 1), selective model specification (such as excluding the 1992 pre-reform wave from the econometric regression) cannot be ruled out in the absence of a registered protocol.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Serious — While the study uses official INE household surveys across Bolivia's four largest cities, survey documentation did not specify the sampling design ('sampling method not specified', Note 13, p. 13; analyzed as simple random samples, p. 4), sample sizes dropped sharply in later waves (most acutely to n = 56 in El Alto in 2001; Table 2, p. 3), and the affordability analysis conditions on post-intervention utility connection ('connected households only', p. 11), which biases cross-period affordability estimates when poor households are disconnected (as occurred in Cochabamba between 2001 and 2005).

domain_ratings.justification: Privatization was assigned non-randomly at the city level across only four cities (La Paz and El Alto vs. Cochabamba and Santa Cruz), as the authors explicitly note (p. 5). Pre-intervention water coverage trajectories during 1992-1996 differed sharply across cities (e.g., lowest-quintile coverage rose 22.3 percentage points in La Paz and 15.9 points in Santa Cruz vs. only 2.2 points in El Alto and 5.1 points in Cochabamba; Table 7, p. 7), violating parallel pre-trends without pre-trend adjustment in the probit DiD model. Covariate adjustment in Table 12 (p. 11) is limited to either household per-capita income (acknowledged as potentially endogenous in Note 17, p. 13) or just three dwelling proxies (rooms, electricity, wall material) due to questionnaire incompatibility (Note 18, p. 13). Unobserved time-varying city shocks, major differences in urban population growth (Figure 3, p. 6), and lack of city-level cluster-robust inference (only 4 city clusters; design df ~ 2,916-3,276 in Table 12) leave substantial confounding risk. Affordability comparisons (2001 vs. 2005) are unadjusted descriptive statistics without a pre-privatization baseline.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 5-8, 11, 13], Section 4 (The Model), Section 5(a)-(b) (Tables 5, 7; Figures 3-4), Section 6 (Table 12), Notes 17-18

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Data come from four repeated cross-sectional INE surveys (1992, 1996, 2001, 2005; Table 2, p. 3) restricted to Bolivia's four largest cities. However, INE dataset documentation did not specify the sampling design (Note 13, p. 13), leading the authors to treat complex survey data as simple random samples for Welch t-tests (p. 4), and city sample sizes fell drastically over time—most severely in El Alto in 2001, which had only n = 56 households (down from 652 in 1992 and 316 in 1996; Table 2, p. 3). Furthermore, the affordability analysis (Tables 10-11, pp. 10-11) restricts the sample to households connected to the utility—conditioning on a post-intervention outcome—which the authors note distorts Cochabamba's apparent affordability improvement because poor households lost connection between 2001 and 2005 (p. 11).

City-level concession status for La Paz and El Alto (privatized under Aguas del Illimani S.A. from July 1997 to 2005) and Santa Cruz (consumer cooperative throughout) is clearly established from regulatory records. However, classifying Cochabamba purely as a 'non-privatized' comparator (pp. 3, 5-6) introduces exposure misclassification/contamination because Cochabamba's water utility was privatized in 1999 under Aguas del Tunari before its contract was cancelled in 2000 amid 'water war' riots and a 35% average tariff hike (pp. 2-3, Table 1). In addition, tariffs in La Paz and El Alto were raised immediately prior to privatization (p. 12; Note 14, p. 13), blurring the pre-reform baseline for tariff/affordability perceptions.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 2-3, 5-6, 12-13], Section 2 (Table 1), Section 3, Section 4, Section 7(b), Notes 11 & 14

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Evaluated as the observational policy effect of adopting private water concessions versus public/cooperative management, substantial unbalanced co-interventions and contextual disruptions occurred across comparator cities during follow-up—most notably Cochabamba's aborted 1999-2000 privatization, civil unrest, and severe post-2001 public-sector coverage contraction (from 78.6% in 2001 to 61.8% in 2005; Table 5, p. 6), alongside nationwide regulatory reforms (1999 Law 2029 and Law 2066 establishing SISAB; Note 6, p. 13). Within La Paz and El Alto, the concessionaire also fell short of contractually mandated connection targets (achieving 64.7% of El Alto targets by 2001 per SISAB's 2005 audit; p. 2), which is part of real-world implementation performance rather than trial protocol non-adherence, but cross-city co-intervention imbalance warrants Moderate concern.

For the primary piped-water access DiD regressions, item-level missingness within the pooled INE survey waves is very low: combined 1996 + 2001 survey N is 3,335 with regression analytic N = 3,240 (income model) and 3,277 (dwelling-wealth model), and combined 1996 + 2005 survey N is 2,945 with regression analytic N = 2,917 and 2,945 (Table 2, p. 3; Table 12, p. 11). However, for the secondary affordability outcome, pre-privatization 1996 expenditure data are completely missing ('A before and after privatization comparison is not possible because of the lack of data for 1996', p. 5), restricting analysis to post-reform waves (2001 and 2005).

Outcomes were extracted from general-purpose INE household surveys, minimizing investigator diagnostic bias, but Table 4 (p. 4) reveals non-equivalent water-access question wording between pre-privatization and post-privatization waves: the 1992 and 1996 surveys explicitly distinguished piped water from the utility network inside the dwelling or yard (and excluded private networks in 1992), whereas the 2001 and 2005 surveys recorded only generic 'Piped water' without specifying utility vs. private network or inside dwelling vs. yard. Protected vs. unprotected wells/boreholes also could not be distinguished (pp. 3-4). For affordability, surveys collected only prior-month monetary spending without volumetric water consumption (pp. 5, 10), making it impossible to separate tariff increases from consumption changes or newly enforced metering/billing of previously unbilled households (Figure 6, p. 10; Note 21, p. 13).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: No pre-analysis plan or pre-registered study protocol is reported in the paper. The authors present descriptive trends across four waves (1992, 1996, 2001, 2005), three Kakwani achievement parameter values (e = 0.1, 0.5, 1), and four probit DiD specifications (two time windows [1996-2001 and 1996-2005] crossed with two wealth specifications; Table 12, p. 11), which shows reasonable analytical transparency, but in the absence of a registered protocol there is no information to verify whether alternative models (e.g., including 1992 pre-trends or alternative functional forms) were explored.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Hailu, Osorio, and Tsukada (2012) conduct a repeated cross-sectional comparative evaluation and difference-in-differences (DiD) probit analysis of water utility privatization in Bolivia (1997-2005 concession in La Paz and El Alto vs. cooperative provision in Santa Cruz de la Sierra and public provision in Cochabamba) using four INE household survey waves (1992, 1996, 2001, 2005), contextualized with secondary regulatory and audit documentation. Appraised with ROBINS-I, the study has a Serious overall risk of bias. Methodological strengths include distributional disaggregation by income quintile, concentration curves/indices, Kakwani achievement indices accounting for baseline coverage ceilings, low item missingness in the water-access regressions, and candid acknowledgment of causal caveats and contractual non-compliance (SISAB's 2005 audit). However, causal inference is seriously constrained by: (D1) non-random policy assignment across only four cities with divergent 1992-1996 pre-trends, limited household covariates due to survey incompatibility, unadjusted time-varying city shocks, and unclustered standard errors; (D2) unspecified INE survey sampling designs, severe sample shrinkage in El Alto in 2001 (n = 56), and conditioning the affordability analysis on post-intervention connection status; and (D6) shifts in survey water-source categories between 1992/1996 and 2001/2005 (Table 4) plus lack of volumetric water consumption data or 1996 baseline expenditure data. Moderate concerns also arise from classifying Cochabamba as a non-privatized control despite its turbulent 1999-2000 privatization (D3/D4), and no pre-analysis plan exists (D7: No information).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Non-randomized comparative policy evaluation using repeated cross-sectional household surveys (1992, 1996, 2001, 2005) and a difference-in-differences (DiD) probit regression model across four Bolivian cities, supplemented by secondary institutional/regulatory background
raw_response.where_found_summary: Institutional and legal context in Section 2 (pp. 2-3, Table 1) and Notes 3-11 (pp. 12-13); survey data sources, sample sizes, water-access definitions, and delivery/equity/affordability methods in Section 3 (pp. 3-5, Tables 2-4) and Notes 12-15 (p. 13); DiD probit specification and causal caveats in Section 4 (pp. 5-6) and Notes 16-18 (p. 13); descriptive delivery, equity, and affordability results in Section 5 (pp. 6-11, Tables 5-11, Figures 3-6) and Appendix A (p. 14); DiD regression results in Section 6 (p. 11, Table 12).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical design is a quantitative non-randomized comparative evaluation of a policy intervention (water utility privatization in La Paz and El Alto vs. comparator utilities in Santa Cruz de la Sierra and Cochabamba) using repeated cross-sectional household microdata before and after reform and an explicit difference-in-differences (DiD) probit regression model (Sections 3-4, pp. 3-6; Section 6, p. 11). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, non-randomized comparative intervention/policy evaluations (including DiD and controlled before-after designs) map directly to ROBINS-I. Although Section 2 and Section 7 discuss institutional and contractual context, those sections draw on secondary literature and regulatory reports rather than primary qualitative fieldwork, so MMAT does not apply.
